transcript:
Meeting header: Date/time: 2025-10-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Recording: auto
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Orion Spark - Lead ML Eng), Tomás Rivera (Orion - DevOps), Priya Shah (Orion - PM)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, hope the calendar time worked, we're Maya, AE on Redwood, and Diego our SE will run the technical bits. Quick agenda: SDK quickstart, auth, sandbox setup, brief Optimize tips and then Q&A.
[00:22] Priya: Yep timing's fine. We wanted to make sure we get the auth story nailed and understand what the devs will need to run the smoke tests.
[00:35] Maya: Great, quick intro from your side?
[00:40] Lena: Sure, I'm Lena. We're building an insights pipeline on top of LLMs for doc summarization; latency target is under 250ms p50 for interactive flows, and P95 under 800 if possible. We'll start with hosted for speed but want a path to VPC/private later.
[01:02] Tomás: I manage infra, we have strict egress policies and want to know about VPC peering or Private deployment. Also KMS integration for keys is must.
[01:18] Diego: Awesome, that'll frame recommendations. I'll show the Python and TS SDK flows and where you wire in API keys vs service accounts. Note: some of my slides say "Redwood Consol"—that's a typo, it's Console.
[01:35] Maya: Ok jumping in. First, quick link we shared: SDK quickstart repo -> https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart (sandbox branch). Also a slides deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/sdk-onboard.pdf (shared).
[01:55] Diego: Opening the repo, top-level README lists environment variables: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_ENV (sandbox/prod), REDWOOD_REGION. For TS there's an npm package @redwood/inference and for Python pip install redwood-inference.
[02:22] Lena: Do you support both streaming and non-streaming? We need streaming for our chat interface.
[02:30] Diego: Yes, both. Example shows stream using ws or SSE depending on SDK. Caveat: streaming on sandbox runs slightly slower due to throttling, but full perf on Dedicated.
[02:48] Tomás: How are creds handled in CI? We use GitHub actions and store secrets in vault.
[02:55] Diego: Two patterns: short-lived service accounts with key rotation via the Console, or injecting REDWOOD_API_KEY at build-time from your vault. We also support SSO-managed service principals for enterprise.
[03:10] Priya: And rotation? We need automated rotation every 30 days ideally.
[03:16] Maya: Rotation is supported, Diego will show where in Console to create service accounts and set rotation policy. For Private, you'll integrate KMS/HSM on your side.
[03:30] Diego: Switching to a live demo. I'm running the Python quickstart: pip install, set REDWOOD_API_KEY, and run sample_generate.py.
[03:45] [screen share audio faint] Diego: You can see the code — client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY"), env="sandbox") then response = client.generate("Summarize this doc")... 
[04:08] [04:10] Diego: The SDK also exposes low-level request options: model, max_tokens, temperature, and batching controls. For batching we have a client.batch API. Example payloads are in examples/benchmarks.
[04:36] Lena: For batching, how do you tune batch size vs latency? Our workloads have lots of short requests from UI.
[04:44] Diego: Short answer: smaller max batch with tight latency SLOs, plus dynamic batching policy. Redwood Optimize will recommend batch size based on traces and token distribution — we'll demo that.
[04:58] Maya: Quick note on model selection — our catalog includes quantized variants for cost savings; you'll see 'redwood-3b-quant' suggested. Slight quality delta, good for high throughput backgrounds.
[05:15] Tomás: Can we pin model versions? We need reproducibility for e2e tests.
[05:22] Diego: Yes, pin by model_version in requests or pin route in Console to a model version for the route.
[05:30] [06:00] Diego: Now TS quickstart — npm i @redwood/inference, import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'. The auth flow mirrors Python. Example uses fetch-based streaming handler.
[06:20] Priya: Any gotchas around CORS for browser clients?
[06:26] Diego: We don't recommend embedding API keys in public client. Typical pattern: call your backend which proxies to Redwood. For private deployments you can run a short-lived proxy inside your VPC.
[06:45] Tomás: Ok makes sense. What about tracing and cost attribution per team?
[06:52] Maya: Console has token-level breakdowns and per-route dashboards. You can attach metadata/tags to requests (team_id, project) and get per-tag metrics in Console. We'll provide an example instrumentation file.
[07:12] Lena: Security stuff — you mentioned SSO and service principals earlier; how does SAML map to service accounts?
[07:20] Diego: Your SAML SSO can map users to RBAC roles in Console. For machine-to-machine we recommend service accounts created in Console, optionally federated via your IdP. For Private, you re-use your KMS and HSM; keys never leave your network.
[07:38] Priya: Is Redwood SOC2 and do you have pen test reports?
[07:42] Maya: Yes we are SOC 2 Type II. I'll send the security bundle after call (we have a redwood-security.zip link in the deck).
[07:55] Tomás: Network egress — we run in a strict environment; does Redwood offer VPC peering or private endpoints?
[08:02] Diego: Yes two options: VPC endpoints for hosted or full Private deployment inside your VPC. Private supports on-prem air-gapped setups. There's some lead time for Private — typically a few weeks for provisioning and cert exchange.
[08:20] Maya: We'll include estimated timelines in the follow-up.
[08:26] [08:30] Diego: Now quick Console tour — creating a route: you can create a route with model pin, concurrency limit, batch policy, and fallback to a cheaper model on capacity pressure. The UI shows live metrics and error traces.
[08:53] Priya: Can we automate route creation via Terraform or API?
[09:00] Diego: Yes both — there's an infra-as-code API and Terraform provider. Example in infra/terraform/ on the repo.
[09:15] Lena: Optimize demo?
[09:18] Diego: Short demo: We ran your sample corpus offline, Redwood Optimize suggested enabling prefix cache and batch size 8 with a 50ms batch window; that reduced token cost by ~28% in our test. Quick screenshot: https://redwood.ai/optimize/reports/orion-sample.png (shared).
[09:45] Tomás: What's prefix caching?
[09:49] Diego: It's KV cache of common prompts or system messages so repeated prefixes don't re-encode each time. Great for chat applications with repeated system role.
[10:05] Lena: For P95 latency concerns, does caching introduce staleness?
[10:12] Diego: Cache TTLs are configurable, and Optimize flags when quality regressions might occur. You can set consistency rules per route.
[10:26] Priya: Any limitations for models that use longer context windows?
[10:32] Diego: Larger context can increase kernel selection cost and memory; runtime auto-selects optimized kernels. For very long contexts we suggest chunking and reranking.
[10:46] [11:00] Maya: Let's talk smoke test plan — Diego will provide a small benchmark script that posts 2000 short requests and measures p50/p95. We'll run in sandbox first.
[11:12] Diego: I'll attach the script in the repo under examples/benchmarks/smoke_test.py and smoke_test.ts. It uses concurrent worker pool default 20, configurable. Use REDWOOD_ENV=sandbox.
[11:30] Tomás: Is sandbox rate-limited? We need to know to interpret results.
[11:36] Diego: Sandbox has softer limits and some throttling. We'll annotate expected delta vs Dedicated — expect ~10–20% slower and occasional 429s in sandbox under heavy load. We'll provide a baseline spreadsheet.
[11:51] Priya: On billing: will sandbox usage be billed to our account?
[11:55] Maya: Sandbox runs on trial credits we allocate. For production, billing is per-token and per-embedding usage; Dedicated has reserved capacity pricing.
[12:10] Lena: One more on logs: do you retain request content in logs? We have PD data concerns.
[12:16] Diego: Data retention policy configurable. For tenant data you can opt out of retention and enable audit logs only. Private guarantees data never leaves your env.
[12:30] [12:35] Priya: Ok on to CI integration, we use GitHub Actions; how to rotate keys automatically?
[12:43] Diego: Use short-lived service account keys and a rotation job that pulls new keys from Console via OIDC flow. Example GH Action in repo: .github/workflows/redwood-rotate.yml.
[13:00] Tomás: For our compliance team, can we restrict which users can create routes or access logs?
[13:06] Maya: Console RBAC supports role granularity — auditors can get read-only log access, Devs can get deploy rights. We'll share role matrix.
[13:20] [13:30] Diego: Quick pitfalls I often see: 1) embedding API keys in frontend; 2) expecting sandbox perf to equal Dedicated; 3) not tagging requests for cost center attribution.
[13:44] Lena: Good callouts.
[13:50] Priya: Any limitations for Japanese or other multi-byte languages?
[13:55] Diego: Models handle multilingual well; Optimize will surface tokenization differences. For embeddings, measure cosine drift.
[14:08] Maya: Let's note blockers — Tomás, you mentioned KMS/HSM and VPC are blockers for production. Anything else?
[14:16] Tomás: Also we need proof of P95 < 800ms under 200 RPS or we'll likely push for Dedicated.
[14:24] Diego: We can try to reproduce that in the perf deep-dive; if not feasible at Hosted we can discuss Dedicated sizing.
[14:36] [15:00] Priya: For our PoC timeline: we want a 2-week smoke test then an internal review. That means samples and creds this week ideally.
[15:10] Maya: We'll prioritize. Action items recap at end.
[15:18] Diego: Quickly opening example code snippet for tagging: client.generate({ input, metadata: { team: 'orion-ml', feature: 'summarize' } }) and Console shows per-metadata usage.
[15:40] Lena: Nice.
[15:48] Maya: Ok wrapping up, recap of next steps and who owns what.
[15:56] Priya: Thanks all.
[16:00] END
